<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Consider how "nature" and "art" are described and related in the opening lines.</Question>
<Question level={2}>When he says "nature" what does he mean?</Question>
<Question level={2}>How is art related to nature? How is it similar to nature or different?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Why is the Leviathan or the State said to be a product of art? How is it an imitation of nature?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>As the State is described, what kind of picture of the human person emerges?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>At the bottom of 117b Hobbes gives a description of his plan for the rest of his book. What does he plan to do?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Regarding the first part of his investigation, he criticizes where others have begun their investigation and instructs us to start elsewhere. Where does he think we should begin?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Does this tell us anything about his procedure?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Is there something distinctively modern about this starting point?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Could he be rejecting the methods of the past in some way? If so, how?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

While I'm not asking you to read chapters 1-4, it is a good idea to look at the titles of these chapters and browse around to get a sense of what Hobbes is up to.

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What definition does Hobbes give to the word "reason" (c. 5, p. 128b)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Why does Hobbes think Philosophers have so often been led into error? What is needed to correct this? (c. 5, p. 130)</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>On p. 131a, Hobbes gives a nice summary of how the mind thinks, how it ensures clarity, and how it proceeds to the "benefit of mankind". What sorts of things are said to prevent us from this clarity and leave humanity without benefit?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>In chapter 6, pay particular attention to what Hobbes defines as "good" (p. 132b).</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>The idea of "fear" becomes important later on in the text, so make sure to identify the definition Hobbes assigns to "Fear" (see p. 133).</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>From chapter 7, be able to distinguish the difference between Opinion, Science, and Belief or Faith.</Question>
<Question level={2}>In whom do we really trust, when we have faith in religious doctrine?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Why does Hobbes show this early concern for religion? Could there be any historical reasons for this concern (Hobbes lived from 1588-1679)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-discussion">
<Question level={1}>What's your reaction to Hobbes's definition of reason? Does it seem different than other conceptions of reason that you've seen in other thinkers? How so?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Does Hobbes's understanding of the "good" seem correct or problematic to you? Is it different from ideas of the good seen in other philosophers?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Make sure you understand Hobbes's conception of the nature of power. What is the greatest form of power?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>How does Hobbes's definition of human worth depend on power?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Please consider carefully paragraphs 1 and 2 of chapter 11. Consider Hobbes's discussion of our restless desire for power. Why is this desire restless?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

While chapter 12 is long, here are four questions to consider. (Note that while the idea of a religious government is very foreign to us in the present, it was a central issue in the English Civil War. Both sides appealed to God as the ultimate political authority and the justification for their claims to power. In keeping with Hobbes's proclivity to break with the past, his aim here is to show that a religious government will not, in the end, work.)

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={2}>What are the four reasons Hobbes gives for why religions have been created?</Question>
<Question level={2}>How are fear and desire essential to Hobbes's understanding of how religion functions and motivates people?</Question>
<Question level={2}>How has religion (and its general origins in ignorance and fear) been used as a means of political control?</Question>
<Question level={2}>What is the eventual problem with government based on religion?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>According to chapter 13, what is the state of nature, and why is equality an essential component of it?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Why does this equality lead to conflict and mistrust (diffidence)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is the best way to defend yourself, if you mistrust everyone else?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What are the "incommodities" of the "state of nature"?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What are the passions that drive us toward peace?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-discussion">
<Question level={1}>In what way do you see "fear" and "power" working together in Hobbes's conception of human of motivation? Can we ever have enough power according to Hobbes? Why or why not?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Contrast Hobbes' understanding of the Right of Nature and the Law of Nature.</Question>
<Question level={2}>How does the Law of Nature seem to follow from the Right of Nature?</Question>
<Question level={2}>How is reason involved here? Why doesn't this Law exist for mere animals?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is the first law of nature? Why would not obeying it usually be a violation of the general Law of Nature?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Are there occasions when the first law of nature need not be obeyed? What are these occasions?</Question>
<Question level={2}>What does this say about the idea of "rights"?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Does our natural right/liberty trump natural laws or do laws trump rights? Is there limit to how far a law can obligate us? What is this limit?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is the second law of nature?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Why does this follow from the injunction of the first?</Question>
<Question level={2}>How does this law begin to combat the culture of fear described in c. 13?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is Hobbes' definition of a contract or a covenant?</Question>
<Question level={2}>What is its relation to the second law of nature?</Question>
<Question level={2}>What is needed for a covenant to be valid rather than void? Why?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is justice? What is injustice?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Why can there be no justice or injustice in the state of nature, and why do these concepts only begin to exist in the Commonwealth? (c. 15)</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>In c. 15:</Question>
<Question level={2}>How do "good" and "evil", "right and wrong", acquire a universal and absolute (non-relative) status in society that they did not have in the state of nature?</Question>
<Question level={2}>What one universal desire in the state of nature grounds this transition?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-discussion">
<Question level={1}>In what ways do you see Hobbes, in chapter 14, urging individuals to settle for something less than perfect? Why does Hobbes think the use of our unrestrained natural right will lead to less freedom and not more? Why does giving up some of our natural freedom, in the end, give us more freedom and not less?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

## Leviathan, cc. 17-19

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is the end or purpose of the commonwealth (c. 17)?</Question>
<Question level={2}>How does this connect to Hobbes' discussion of the need for covenants and the difficulty of making a "valid" covenant in c. 14 and 15?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Why can't human beings be like bees (c. 17)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is the "scientific" definition of a commonwealth (c. 17)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>How does the commonwealth come into existence?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Is the covenant that produces the commonwealth a "valid covenant"?</Question>
<Question level={2}>If so, why is this covenant valid, while prior to this covenant, "valid covenants" seemed impossible? In other words, what is unique about this covenant (c. 17)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is distinctive about a commonwealth that comes to be through an act of Instituting (c. 18)?</Question>
<Question level={2}>How might this differ from other aggregates of people or factions?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What are the consequences of such an Institution (i.e. what rights belong to the Sovereign)?</Question>
<Question level={2}>Consider one or two of the rights of the Sovereign and why this right necessarily follows from the nature of the Instituted commonwealth (c. 18)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Why must the dissenting vote also recognize the elected sovereign (c. 18)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-discussion">
<Question level={1}>At the close of chapter 18, Hobbes notes that the reader might complain that life under the Sovereign seems very miserable. First, having read this far in his book, what is your reaction to the society he describes? Is it a society you would want to live in? Why or why not? Second, how does his response to the objection affect your own opinion? Is he right that we complain only because we have on "multiplying glasses" rather than "prospective glasses"?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

## Leviathan, c. 26

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What are Civil Laws?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>How are they related to Laws of Nature?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>How are Civil and Natural Laws contained within each other and yet still distinct (c. 26, p. 209a, paragraph 8)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Consider Hobbes' discussion of making and interpreting the Civil Laws (c. 26, pp. 212-213, paragraphs, 20-24).</Question>
<Question level={2}>Why must the Sovereign alone perform these functions?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Do Natural Laws need to be written down? Why or why not?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>Do Civil Laws need to be written down? Why or why not?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is the difference between Natural and Positive Laws (c. 26, p. 215b paragraph 37)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What does Hobbes have to say about the Divine Law (c. 26, p. 216, paragraph 40)?</Question>
<Question level={2}>What are the possible problems with Divine Law?</Question>
<Question level={2}>To what extent are we ever obligated to it?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-content">
<Question level={1}>What is the difference between a Fundamental Law and a Non-Fundamental Law (c. 26, p. 217, paragraph 43)?</Question>
</QuestionBlock>

<QuestionBlock type="reading-discussion">
<Question level={1}>As this is our last day with Hobbes's own text, consider what questions still linger for you? What still isn't quite clear and why? Are there aspects of Hobbes' system that seem unconvincing to you? Are there aspects of Hobbes' text that seem really insightful to you? Explain why.</Question>
</QuestionBlock>
